rewritten_text:
I cannot describe the joy I felt in turning away from political quarrels in my country and bodily suffering abroad to my own beloved home. Here was a place devoted to goodness and love, to peace and the sharing of our deepest feelings. Had I never left Windsor, I would not have felt this so strongly. But in Greece I had suffered fear and terrible upheaval. After a time of anxiety and sorrow there, I had lost two people whose very names represented greatness and virtue. Surely such troubles could never invade the family circle still left to me, while we lived quietly, sheltered in our dear forest. The passing years did bring a few changes, of course. Time, as always, left reminders of death upon our pleasures and hopes. Idris, the most affectionate wife, sister, and friend, was also a tender, loving mother. Motherhood was no pastime to her, as it is to many; it was a passion. We had had three children. The second had died while I was in Greece. This loss had mixed her triumphant joy in motherhood with grief and fear. Before it happened, the little creatures born from her, who would carry on her brief life, had seemed certain to live. Now she feared that merciless death might take her remaining darlings as it had taken their brother. The smallest illness terrified her. Any separation from them made her miserable. She had placed all her happiness in their fragile lives and watched constantly, afraid that the stealthy thief would again steal her precious treasures. Fortunately, she had little reason to worry. Alfred, now nine, was an honest, brave little boy with a bright face, gentle eyes, and a nature both kind and independent. Our youngest was still a baby, but his soft cheeks glowed with health, and his tireless energy filled our home with innocent laughter.

Clara had grown beyond the age whose inability to understand or speak caused Idris such anxiety. She was dear to Idris and to everyone. Intelligence blended in her with innocence, sensitivity with patience, and seriousness with unfailing good humor. Her extraordinary beauty came with such lovable simplicity that she seemed a pearl among our treasured possessions, wonderful and precious.

At the start of winter, our nine-year-old Alfred went to Eton for the first time. He saw this as his first step toward manhood and was delighted. Studying and playing with other boys brought out his finest qualities: steady determination, generosity, and firmness tempered by self-control.

The stars still shone brightly when I woke, and Taurus high in the southern sky told me it was midnight. My dreams had been troubled. I imagined myself invited to Timon’s final feast. I arrived hungry; the dishes were uncovered, and hot water released its uninviting steam. I fled the host’s anger, but the host had become Raymond. To my feverish imagination, the vessels he hurled after me overflowed with foul vapor, while my friend’s body twisted into a thousand forms and swelled into an enormous apparition, the mark of plague upon its forehead. The growing shadow rose higher and higher, filling the unbreakable dome that arched above the world, supporting and enclosing it, and then seeming to strain beyond it. The nightmare became torture. With a fierce effort I shook off sleep and restored my mind to its ordinary workings. My first thought was of Perdita. I must return to her and sustain her, finding whatever nourishment despair could offer her wounded heart. Through the stern demands of duty and the gentle tenderness of remembrance, I must call her back from grief’s wild extremes.

The stars were my only guide. I turned away from the dreadful ruins of the Golden City and, after great exertion, managed to escape its boundaries. Outside the walls I met a company of soldiers, borrowed a horse from one of them, and hurried to my sister. In this short time the plain had changed. The camp had been dismantled, and scattered remnants of the disbanded army gathered in small groups. Every face was troubled; every movement expressed shock and dismay.

I entered the palace with a heavy heart and stood afraid to move, speak, or look. Perdita sat in the middle of the hall on the marble floor, her head bowed against her chest, her hair disordered, her fingers twisting restlessly together. She was as pale as the marble, and anguish tightened every feature. She noticed me and looked up questioningly. The faint hope in her glance was agony to see. The words died before I could speak them, and I felt a ghastly smile crease my lips. She understood my expression. Her head dropped again, and her fingers resumed their restless movements. At last I found my voice, but its sound terrified her. The unhappy girl had read my face; nothing could make her willing to hear her terrible misfortune given shape and confirmed in hard, irreversible words. She even seemed eager to turn my thoughts away from it. Rising from the floor, she whispered, “Hush! Clara has cried so much, and now she is sleeping. We must not wake her.”

During his brief visit, Emma had hardly seen him. Still, she had seen enough to get their first meeting over with and to feel that the mixture of wounded pride and self-importance in his manner did him no favors. In fact, she was beginning to wonder how she had ever found him pleasant. Seeing him brought up so many uncomfortable feelings that she would have welcomed the promise of never meeting him again, except for the moral benefit of the experience: a penance, a lesson, a useful blow to her pride. She wished him well, but he caused her pain. Knowing he was happy twenty miles away would have pleased her most.

His marriage, however, would certainly make his continued presence in Highbury less painful. It would remove many pointless worries and ease many awkward situations. A Mrs. Elton would provide a reason for any change in their relations. Their former closeness could fade without comment. They could almost begin their polite acquaintance over again.

Emma gave little thought to the woman herself. No doubt she was good enough for Mr. Elton, educated and talented enough for Highbury, and pretty enough—though probably plain beside Harriet. As for her family connections, Emma felt completely satisfied. Despite all his boasts about his own importance and his contempt for Harriet, she was certain he had gained nothing there. The facts on that subject seemed possible to discover. What sort of woman she was remained uncertain, but her family background could be investigated. Apart from her ten thousand pounds, she did not seem superior to Harriet at all. She brought no famous name, distinguished ancestry, or important relations. Miss Hawkins was the younger of two daughters of a Bristol man whom one must, of course, call a merchant. Yet the modest total earnings of his business life made it reasonable to suppose his trade had been equally modest in status. She usually spent part of each winter in Bath, but Bristol was her home—the very center of Bristol. Her parents had died some years earlier, yet an uncle remained, employed “in the law.” No one ventured any more respectable description of his work than that. She had lived with him. Emma guessed he did menial work for an attorney and lacked the intelligence to advance. All the family’s grandeur seemed to rest on the elder sister, who had married very well: a prosperous gentleman near Bristol who owned two carriages! That completed the story. That was the great glory of Miss Hawkins.
